1. Introduction
Weilin Zhang, Jinbo Zan

Asia is a mosaic of continental blocks and accretionary systems amalgamated together along sutures marking
Investigation: Liang Yu, Maodu Yan,
Chong Guan, Qiang Fu, Wanlong Xu, lost oceans. One of the most important of these ancient oceans—the Paleo-Tethys—was an immense Paleozo-

In its eastern half, the Paleo-Tethys separated a collection of proto-Asian continental blocks in the north (the
Yan, Mathew Domeier, Chong Guan,
Miaomiao Shen, Qiang Fu, Wanlong Xu, Asiatic Hunic terranes of Stampfli et al., 2002) from the northeast margin of Gondwana in the south (G. C. Zhao
Zhichao Niu, Rendeng Shi, Weilin Zhang, et al., 2018). A common first-order narrative envisions the Paleo-Tethys as a single, wedge-shaped basin that
Dawen Zhang, Bingshuai Li
ultimately closed by the arrival of a ribbon-shaped string of Gondwana-derived microcontinents (the Cimmerian

terranes) to the southern margin of Laurasia and proto-Asia in the Mesozoic. However, in the east, the structure
of the Paleo-Tethys and its closure was probably more complex, involving at least two oceanic basins, or ‘branch-
es’ of the Paleo-Tethys. A northern branch, which is often called the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean (or the Mianlue
Ocean), separated the Tarim (TB), Qaidam, Central Qilian, Alxa (or Alex) and North China (NCB) blocks in

The Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean appeared at least by mid-Paleozoic time and in the late Paleozoic and may have
Visualization: Liang Yu, Mathew
Domeier, Wanlong Xu, Jinbo Zan, spanned a width of more than 5,000 km (Guan et al., 2021). This once-expansive ocean ultimately closed when
Bingshuai Li the Gondwana-derived EQT collided with the TB and the NCB, but the specific timing of that event remains
Writing – original draft: Liang Yu,
critically uncertain (e.g., Guan et al., 2021; Reid et al., 2005; P. P. Song et al., 2015; M. D. Yan et al., 2016; Zi
Maodu Yan
Writing – review & editing: Maodu et al., 2012). On the basis of a variety of approaches (e.g., paleontologic, paleomagnetic, magmatic, sedimen-
Yan, Mathew Domeier, Chong Guan, tologic, structural), proposed closure times for the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean range from the late Permian (Sha
Miaomiao Shen, Qiang Fu, Wanlong
& Fürsich, 1999) to the Early–Middle Triassic (Pullen et al., 2008; Zi et al., 2012), the Late Triassic (Guan
Xu, Zunbo Xu, Liye Yang, Rendeng Shi,
Weilin Zhang, Jinbo Zan, Dawen Zhang, et al., 2021; Li, 2008; P. P. Song et al., 2015; M. D. Yan et al., 2016), and the latest Triassic–Early Jurassic (Liu,
Bingshuai Li Tan, et al., 2019; Roger et al., 2010; Tan et al., 2020; L. Y. Zhang et al., 2014). Clearly there is a need for more
precise and direct constraints on the timing of this important event.
The closure of east-west oriented oceans can be quantitatively established from paleomagnetism, which can de-
termine the latitudinal drift history (and eventual collision) of the continental blocks bordering an ocean. Given
that the EQT is immediately south of the Jinshajiang Suture Zone (Figure 1a), its drift history is important to
understand the evolution and closure of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean. A number of Permian to Triassic paleomag-
netic studies have already been carried out in the EQT in order to detail the evolution of the Paleo-Jinshajiang
Ocean (e.g., Cheng et al., 2012, 2013; Guan et al., 2021; K. N. Huang et al., 1992; X. Z. Li et al., 1999; Lin &
Watts, 1988; Ma et al., 2019; C. Y. Song et al., 2012; P. P. Song et al., 2015, 2017, 2020; X. F. Yang et al., 2017;
Zhou et al., 2019; see Figure S1 in Supporting Information S1 for locations). However, collectively, these data
only constrain the closure time of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean to between ∼240 and 209 Ma (Guan et al., 2021),
and so again a more precise estimate of its timing of closure is needed.
In this study, we report new joint paleomagnetic and U-Pb geochronologic data from Late Triassic volcanic rocks
of the EQT. Based on these new data and a synthesis of reported paleomagnetic data and other relevant geological
constraints, we further describe the drift history of the EQT during the Permian and Triassic and more precisely
estimate the closure time of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean in this region.
2. Geological Setting and Sampling
The EQT (alternatively called the ‘North Qiangtang Terrane’ in the literature) comprises one half of the larger,
elongate Qiangtang Terrane, which varies in width from ∼500 km in its mid-section to ∼150 km in its eastern
and western ends (Figure 1a). To the south, the EQT is separated from the Western Qiangtang Terrane (WQT;
alternatively called the ‘South Qiangtang Terrane’) by the so-called Longmu Tso-Shuanghu Suture Zone, and
to the north and northeast the Jinshajiang Suture Zone separates the EQT from the Songpan-Ganzi Terrane and
the Yidun Terrane, respectively (e.g., BGMRXAR, 1993; C. Li et al., 2009; Y. Liu et al., 2011; Metcalfe, 2013;
Pan et al., 2004; Zhang, Cai, et al., 2006; Zhang, Zhang et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2013; Figure 1a). Note that the
east-west continuity of the Jinshajiang Suture Zone across the length of the EQT is a matter of some debate,
particularly east and west of the Zhiduo area. It is also worth noting that despite bearing the same ‘Qiangtang’
label, the EQT and WQT were probably independent of each other in late Paleozoic time: the WQT hosts Per-
mo–Carboniferous glaciomarine diamictites and cold-water biota of Gondwana-affinity whereas the EQT hosts
Permo–Carboniferous carbonates with warmer-water faunas of Cathyasian affinity (Y. C. Zhang et al., 2013). It
is presently unknown what comprises the basement of the EQT, and the oldest exposed rocks in the terrane are
meta-sedimentary rocks of the Early Ordovician Ningduo Group. The Ningduo Group is unconformably overlain
by Late Devonian to late Permian strata, but the most widespread sedimentary sequences in the EQT are of Mes-
ozoic and Cenozoic age (Z. Z. Zhao et al., 2001).

### page_4
Geophysical Research Letters 10.1029/2021GL096902
Our study is focused on the Zhiduo area, which is located in the Qamdo region that is adjacent to the Jinshajiang
Suture Zone in the east of the EQT (Figure 1a). In this area, the principal lithologic units comprise the Carbonif-
erous to early-middle Permian Duocai ophiolitic mélange (sandstone, slate and volcanic rock), the Early–Middle
Triassic Jielong Formation (breccia and bioclastic limestone), the Late Triassic Bolila Formation (biolimestone
and limestone breccia), and the Late Triassic Batang Group, above which late Cenozoic deposits locally lie un-
conformably (the Neogene Quguo Formation and Quaternary deposits; QGSI, 2005a; X. M. Zhao et al., 2006;
Figures 1b and 1c). The Batang Group is widely distributed in the Zhiduo area, which is bounded by the Duocai
ophiolitic mélange to the north and the Bolila Formation to the south. The Batang Group can be further divid-
ed into three formations: the Lower Clastic, the Middle Volcanic and the Upper Limestone Batang formations
(QGSI, 2014; X. M. Zhao et al., 2006). The Middle Volcanic Batang Formation is considered to be a temporal
correlative of the Bolila Formation limestone (QGSI, 2005a; Figure 1c). Abundant fossils, including brachiopods
(e.g., Rhaetinopsis pentagonalis Ching, Oxycolpella elongata Ching et Fang, Amphiclina sp., Arcestes sp.), bi-
valves (Pteria angusta (Saurin), Neomegalodon (N.) sp.), corals (Montlivaltia norica Frech, Thecosmilia sinensis
Liao et Li, Pinacophyllum sp.) and ammonites (Paratibetites sp.), have been observed within the Lower Clastic
and Upper Limestone Batang formations in the Zhiduo area. These fossils constrain the age of the Batang Group
to the Late Triassic (Carnian–Norian) and indicate its deposition occurred in a shallow marine environment
(QGSI, 2014; X. M. Zhao et al., 2006).
The Middle Volcanic Batang Formation is well exposed in the Zhiduo area (Figure 1b), due to regional NW-trend-
ing faults. The exposure of the formation extends more than 10 km laterally, and it presents a thickness of up to
1,000 m. It consists mainly of basalt, rhyolitic tuff, rhyolite, dacite, and crystal tuff, and is intercalated with some
limestone and siltstone layers (QGSI, 2014; X. M. Zhao et al., 2006). The Middle Volcanic Batang Formation has
conformable contacts with both the underlying Lower Clastic and overlying Upper Limestone Batang formations.
Two recent U-Pb zircon dating results from dacites and rhyolites of the Middle Volcanic Batang Formation in the
Zhiduo area have yielded crystallization ages of 227 ± 2 Ma (Liu, Tan, et al., 2019) and 221 ± 1 Ma (S. Q. Zhao
et al., 2014; Figure 1b). Given the clear bedding of the formation and the fact that it was emplaced within the
critical age range that we are interested in (∼240–209 Ma), we elected to target the thick Middle Volcanic Batang
Formation for paleomagnetic study.
We collected samples from the Middle Volcanic Batang Formation at the Duocai section (33.8°N, 95.2°E) along
the Riari oblique syncline in Zhiduo. In this section, the volcanic rocks mostly comprise lithic-crystal tuff and
crystal tuff (Figures S2e and S2f in Supporting Information S1). The syncline has a NW-SE-trending axis with a
northeast limb dipping ∼25°–53° toward the southwest and a southwest limb dipping ∼52° toward the northeast.
Given the absence of Jurassic-Cretaceous sediments in the Zhiduo area, the exact time of folding cannot be con-
strained. However, in the adjacent Zaduo area, an angular unconformity is observed between Late Triassic strata
and the Middle Jurassic Quemocuo Formation (QGSI, 2014), which implies that a major phase of deformation
occurred in the region during the Late Triassic or Early Jurassic. We collected paleomagnetic samples from both
fold limbs in the Duocai section, which is over 200 m thick. Eight to twelve core samples were collected at each
site with the use of a portable gasoline-powered drill. The paleomagnetic samples were oriented with a magnet-
ic compass and also a sun compass when weather allowed. A total of 131 core samples of tuff were collected
from 13 sampling sites (sites 1–4 and 8–11 come from the southwest limb and sites 5–7, 12 and 13 come from
northeast limb; Figures S2a–S2d and S2g in Supporting Information S1). In addition, samples of crystal tuff and
lithic-crystal tuff were collected for U-Pb geochronology from the stratigraphic lower (Duocai A) and upper parts
(Duocai B) of the section (Figure 1c and Figure S2g in Supporting Information S1).
3. Zircon U–Pb Geochronology
Zircons were extracted from the two bulk samples using routine crushing and heavy mineral separation tech-
niques at the Yu-Neng Technology Service Limited Company for rock and mineral separation, Langfang, China.
Transmitted and reflected light photomicrographs and cathodoluminescence (CL) images were obtained to ana-
lyze the internal textures of the zircons and to select target sites for U-Pb dating. Zircon U-Pb geochronologic
analyses were conducted at the State Key Laboratory of Tibetan Plateau Earth System, Resources and Environ-
ment, Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing, China, using laser ablation
inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS). In this study, zircon standards 91500 and GJ-1
were used as our primary and secondary standards to determine the U-Th-Pb ratios, and NIST SRM 610 was used

as an external standard to calibrate the Pb concentrations. Isotope ratios and concentrations were obtained by us-
ing the GLITTER 4.0 software (Griffin et al., 2008). In this study, we apply a <10% discordance filter to the gen-
erated data. U-Pb concordia diagrams and weighted average plots were made using Isoplot 4.0 (Ludwig, 2012).
The CL images show that the zircon grains from both samples (Duocai A and Duocai B) are generally transparent,
euhedral or subhedral, and have a prismatic shape with clear oscillatory zoning (Figures S3a and S3d in Support-
ing Information S1). The lengths of the long axes of the grains are 60–150 μm and their Th/U ratios are between
∼0.3 and 0.8, consistent with a magmatic origin (Table S1 in the Supporting Information S1). Analyses of 23 and
19 zircon grains yield a weighted mean 206Pb/238U age of 227.7 ± 3.7 Ma (2σ; MSWD = 0.19) for the stratigraphic
lower sample (Duocai A) and 222.5 ± 3.9 Ma (2σ; MSWD = 0.117) for the stratigraphic upper sample (Duocai
B; Figure S3 in Supporting Information S1), respectively.
These two U-Pb zircon ages from the lower and upper parts of the Duocai section suggest that the sampled Mid-
dle Volcanic Batang Formation ranges in age at least from ∼227 to 222 Ma. This age range is consistent with
both the Carnian–Norian biostratigraphic age estimate on the Batang Group in the Zhiduo region (QGSI, 2014;
X. M. Zhao et al., 2006), and with the two existing U-Pb zircon ages of 227 ± 2 Ma (Liu, Tan, et al., 2019) and
221 ± 1 Ma (S. Q. Zhao et al., 2014; Figure 1b) from the Middle Volcanic Batang Formation in the vicinity of
the study area.
4. Paleomagnetic Results
Rock magnetic experiments and paleomagnetic treatments are described in Text S1 and S2 in the Supporting
Information S1. In summary, these rock magnetic results suggest that SD–PSD magnetite is the main magnet-
ic carrier (in a few cases also with hematite) in the Middle Volcanic Batang Formation in the Duocai section
(Figure S4 in Supporting Information S1). A total of 86 out of 132 samples yielded stable ChRM directions that
fulfill our quality criteria (Text S2 in Supporting Information S1), allowing the definition of a site mean from 11
out of the 13 sites collected. Of these 11 sites, 7 exhibit dual-polarity directions, whereas the other 4 have only
normal polarity directions. Together, they provide an overall mean direction of D = 62.5°, I = 58.7°, k = 2.6,
g g g
α = 36.2° in-situ, and D = 38.9°, I = 51.9°, k = 45.3, and α = 6.9° after tilt correction (Figure 2c, Tables S3
95 s s s 95
and S4 in Supporting Information S1). With tilt-correction, these data yield positive McFadden (1990) and Wat-
son and Enkin (1993) foldtests, a positive McFadden and McElhinny (1990) reversal test (see details in Text S3
of Supporting Information S1), and pass a paleosecular variation check (Text S3 in Supporting Information S1).
Collectively, these results suggest that the ChRM likely represents a primary magnetization. These data yield a
paleopole of 57.6°N, 176.4°E, A = 7.8°, which corresponds to a paleolatitude of 32.5° ± 7.8°N for the study
95
area (Table S4 in Supporting Information S1).
5. Discussion
5.1. Paleomagnetic Constraints on the Permian-Triassic Drift of the EQT
To date, a total of 18 Permian to Triassic paleomagnetic results have been reported from the EQT (Cheng
et al., 2012, 2013; Guan et al., 2021; K. N. Huang et al., 1992; X. Z. Li et al., 1999; Lin & Watts, 1988; Ma
et al., 2019; C. Y. Song et al., 2012; P. P. Song et al., 2015, 2017, 2020; X. F. Yang et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2019)
which present quantitative constraints on its drift history. However, these data are of variable quality and a de-
tailed evaluation by Guan et al. (2021) determined that only five of the poles are of sufficiently high quality to be
of use in reconstructing the drift history of the EQT (Table S5 in Supporting Information S1). According to these
constraints, the EQT was located in the low latitudes of the Southern Hemisphere in the early Permian (∼22°S at
∼297 Ma; P. P. Song et al., 2017), but drifted rapidly northward to cross the equator in the latest Permian (∼5°S
at ∼259 Ma and ∼11°N at ∼251 Ma; Guan et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019), and reached ∼25°N by ∼240 Ma (P. P.
Song et al., 2020) and then reached ∼35°N by the latest Triassic (at ∼209 Ma; P. P. Song et al., 2015; Figures 3a
and 3b).
In Figure 3b, we compare this latitudinal drift history of the EQT against paleolatitude curves for Eurasia, the
Tarim Block (TB) and India (Gondwana), as computed for the same reference location (Table S6 in Supporting
Information S1). As can be seen from these comparisons, the EQT was located some 3,000 km north of the In-
dian margin of Gondwana in the earliest Permian, which is consistent with the observation that the EQT hosts

Figure 2. Equal-area projections of the viscous overprint (low-temperature (field) component) directions (a), characteristic
remnant magnetization directions of specimens (b) and site mean directions (c) for the Middle Volcanic Batang

warm-water Cathyasian faunas of this age (in contrast to the WQT, which hosts cold-water Cimmerian/Gond-
wanan biotas of Permo–Carboniferous age). At the same time, the EQT was also then separated from Eurasia
and the TB by a wide Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean that latitudinally spanned at least 5,000 km (Figure 3b). However,
once the EQT began to drift rapidly northward from mid-Permian time, the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean began to
shrink, and by the Middle Triassic the EQT was only ∼1,000 km from margin of the TB. It could be anticipated
that the collision between the EQT and the TB followed shortly thereafter, and Guan et al. (2021) inferred their
collision to have occurred at ∼230 Ma by extrapolating the northward drift of the EQT into the Late Triassic.
However, among these existing data, the next oldest direct paleomagnetic constraint on the EQT, which yields a

### page_8
Geophysical Research Letters 10.1029/2021GL096902
and reversals tests and the Late Triassic host rocks are well-dated. The new paleomagnetic pole (57.6°N, 176.4°E,
A = 7.8°) fulfills all seven of the reliability criteria of Van der Voo (1990) and Meert et al. (2020) and thus can
95
provide a robust estimate of the position of the EQT at ∼227–222 Ma (mean of ∼225 Ma). At the reference locali-
ty (33.8°N, 95.2°E), this result corresponds to a paleolatitude of ∼32.5 ± 7.8°N (Figures 3a and 3b; pole #5). This
paleolatitude is indistinguishable from the average Permian–Triassic paleolatitude of the TB (∼33.8° ± 4.4°N, B.
C. Huang et al., 2018; Table S6 in Supporting Information S1), suggesting that closure of the Paleo-Jinshajiang
Ocean by collision of the EQT and the TB/Songpan-Ganzi/Yidun Terrane had occurred at least by (but possibly
prior to) 227–222 Ma (Figure 3). This constraint is thus consistent with a ∼230 Ma collision, as inferred by Guan
et al. (2021) from their extrapolation of a constant northward drift of the EQT since the Permian.
5.2. Insights Into the Closure Time of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean
While our new paleomagnetic result presents a key constraint on the closure time of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean,
we note some important caveats associated with this simple analysis. First, the Jinshajiang Suture Zone marks
the divide between the EQT (to the south) and Songpang-Ganzi and Yidun terranes (to the north and northeast),
but there are no reliable Triassic paleomagnetic data available from the latter terranes and so we can only com-
pare results from the EQT and the TB (which do not directly share a suture). Second, a shallow inclination bias
is commonly observed among Cretaceous–Cenozoic sedimentary rocks of Central Asia (including the TB) and
the Triassic paleomagnetic data from the TB are mostly derived from clastic sedimentary rocks (B. C. Huang
et al., 2018), so the possibility of a shallow inclination bias cannot be ruled out. If the Triassic data from the TB
are contaminated by such bias, the collision of the EQT and the TB could have occurred later than ∼230 Ma.
Notably, B. C. Huang et al. (2018) argued that such bias was not likely significant given the occurrence of similar
paleomagnetic directions in Jurassic sedimentary and igneous rocks from the TB (but see also Wu et al., 2017),
and in the absence of demonstrated bias, we have here used their compilation, unaltered. Nevertheless, future
work on the acquisition of new high-quality Triassic paleomagnetic data from the TB and the terranes between it
and the EQT are clearly needed to provide more robust constraints.
Geological estimates of the closure time of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean vary in the literature from at least the
late Permian to the Jurassic. This range can be attributed, at least in part, to the use of different methods which
track different processes (e.g., paleontologic, magmatic, geochemical, sedimentologic, structural), but also to
disagreements about the location and lateral continuation of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean. Nevertheless, along
the Jinshajiang Suture Zone, which we are concerned with herein, there are a number of observations that are
consistent with a Late Triassic closure of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean.
The maximum closure time of an ocean can be determined from the age of the youngest ophiolitic material
preserved within the suture, which must pre-date final suturing. In the Zhiduo area, mafic rocks as young as
∼234 ± 3 Ma (U-Pb on zircon) have been reported from the ophiolitic mélange in the suture zone (B. Liu
et al., 2016) and the occurrence of ocean island basalts with ages spanning from ∼422 to 236 Ma (U-Pb on zircon)
confirms that the suture represents a major, long-lived ocean (Liu, Xiao, et al., 2019) prior to ∼234 Ma. To the
east of the Zhiduo area, ophiolitic material in the Jinshajiang Suture Zone is mostly of Carboniferous age, but ages
as young as ∼294 Ma have been reported (Wang et al., 2000; Zi et al., 2012), whereas to the west of the Zhiduo
area, the youngest ages are Triassic: ∼246 ± 5.18 Ma (K-Ar on diabase; Y. Li et al., 2003) and ∼232 ± 11 Ma
(Sm-Nd isochron from metagabbro; N. Zhang et al., 2012). Collectively, these observations suggest that the
Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean remained open through the late Paleozoic and into the beginning of the Triassic.
The timing of ocean closure can also be constrained from structural and sedimentologic evidence of the con-
tinent-continent collision concluding it. Along the Jinshajiang Suture Zone in the Qamdo region, prominent
unconformities have been reported between the Middle Triassic Jielong Formation and the Late Triassic Jieza
Group in the Zaduo and Zhiduo area (QGSI, 2005a, 2005b), and between the Early−Middle Triassic Malasong-
duo Formation and the Late Triassic Jiapila Formation in the Markam area (TARGS, 2007). In the suture itself
in the Yushu area, ophiolitic rocks including a Late Triassic mélange are thrusted over a Late Triassic matrix
(Dewey et al., 1988; Metcalfe, 1996) and Late Triassic structural fabrics have been dated to ∼230.5 ± 0.8 Ma
by Ar-Ar on phengite (T. N. Yang et al., 2012). In the Gonjo area to the southeast, Middle Triassic eclogites
(∼240 ± 3 Ma and ∼244 ± 1 Ma; U-Pb on zircon) have been discovered in the suture zone, some of which are
hosted by a ∼226 Ma (U-Pb on zircon) adamellite, implying that they were rapidly exhumed in latest Middle to
early Late Triassic time (Tang et al., 2020). To the north, in the Songpan-Ganzi Terrane, the Late Triassic was

### page_9
Geophysical Research Letters 10.1029/2021GL096902
likewise marked by deformation (∼230−200 Ma; Harrowfield & Wilson, 2005) and the initiation of non-marine
deposition. Other sedimentologic evidence of a Late Triassic collision include the appearance of Late Triassic
(Rhaetian palynological age) molasse unconformably above Early−Middle Triassic rocks along the northern
margin of the EQT—which has been attributed to the development of a foreland basin associated with collision of
the EQT against Songpan-Ganzi Terrane (BGMRXAR, 1993; Y. Li et al., 2003)—and the initiation of sediment
mixing between those terranes already by Carnian time (Ding et al., 2013; Gong et al., 2021). Looking further
afield, G. C. Zhao et al. (2018) recently presented a regional geologic synthesis arguing that the East Kunlun (to
the north of the Jinshajiang Suture Zone) and the Mianlue-Qinling and Dabie-Sulu areas (to the east) all signify
closure of the regional Mianlue (e.g., Paleo-Jinshajiang) Ocean at ∼240–220 Ma. Together, these observations
are consistent with a Late Triassic closure of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean.
Many arguments for a younger (Early Jurassic) closure of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean are predicated on in-
terpretations of the magmatic record. The closure of an ocean necessitates the consumption of oceanic litho-
sphere by subduction, and so the timing of arc-related magmatism and its replacement by syn- to post-colli-
sional magmatism can be used to constrain the age of closure. Unfortunately, while there are an abundance of
Triassic igneous rocks in the northern EQT and southern Songpan-Ganzi Terrane, the tectonic environment of
their emplacement—as mostly inferred from geochemistry—remains a topic of active debate. For example, in
the eastern Songpan-Ganzi Terrane, H. F. Zhang et al. (2007) have interpreted ∼211 Ma A-type granites to be
post-collisional, whereas Yuan et al. (2010) interpreted ∼224−205 Ma adakitic and shoshonitic plutons in the
eastern Songpan-Ganzi Terrane to result from crustal thickening during collision, and L. Y. Zhang et al. (2014)
related ∼225−193 Ma I-type granitoids in the western Songpan-Ganzi Terrane to ongoing subduction. Although
it is beyond the scope of the present study to dissect the various geochemical arguments presented for these rocks
as well as the Triassic igneous rocks along the north of the EQT, we note that our new paleomagnetic result can
contribute to this discussion by placing these magmatic episodes in a more well-defined paleogeographic context.
In summary, a range of geological evidence (see Figure S1 in Supporting Information S1 for locations, Table
S7 in Supporting Information S1) from along the Jinshajiang Suture Zone and our new paleomagnetic results
(together with the existing ones) are consistent with a Late Triassic (∼230 Ma) closure of the Paleo-Jinshajiang
Ocean. On the other hand, the paleolatitudinal histories of the TB, Songpan-Ganzi Terrane and Yidun Terrane
remain poor to unconstrained in early Mesozoic time, and so important uncertainties remain about this specific
timing and the potential diachroneity of Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean. Future research dedicated to acquiring new
paleomagnetic constraints from these blocks to supplement the now well-resolved Permian and Triassic paleolat-
itudinal history of the EQT will be decisive in addressing these outstanding questions.
6. Conclusions
Zircon U-Pb dating of two volcanic samples from the upper and lower Middle Volcanic Batang Formation
demonstrates that these rocks were erupted in the Late Triassic, between ∼227 and 222 Ma. A paleomagnetic
investigation of these rocks, involving detailed rock magnetism, field stability tests and paleosecular variation
analysis, suggests that they maintain a primary Late Triassic magnetization. On the basis of paleomagnetic results
from 11 sites (86 samples), we report a robust ∼225 Ma paleomagnetic pole of 57.6°N and 176.4°E (A = 7.8°). 95
This result indicates that the EQT occupied a paleolatitude of 32.5 ± 7.8°N (reference point at 33.8°N and
95.2°E) in the early Late Triassic. Integrated with other reliable paleomagnetic data from the region, and in the
context of independent geologic evidence, we ascertain that the EQT collided with the TB/Songpan-Ganzi/Yidun
Terrane, and thereby closed the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean in the Qamdo region, before 227–222 Ma, and most
likely at ∼230 Ma.
